title: Разбитая бутылка и шантаж  (The Broken Bottle and Blackmail)

segments.t: Back in the kitchen, Max confronts Kostya and learns that Kristina intentionally smashed an expensive bottle of wine and blamed Kostya for it. When Max admits that Kristina will fire Kostya unless Max sleeps with her, Nastya overhears the whole conversation.
Ну что.
С кем не бывает.
Ну, опоздал, ну, я больше не буду.
Не очень.
Я хотел еще вчера вам об этом сообщить.
Но мы ж трубку не брали.
Елена Павловна!
Макс, кто разбил бутылку?
В смысле?
Кристина ее разбила и сказала, что тебя уволит.
Если я с ней не пересплю.
С кем с Настей?
С Кристиной?
Alright, let's go through it step by step in English.
Ну что.
'Well then.' The grammar packs 'come on' and 'what' into a tight, idiomatic kitchen exchange.
С кем не бывает.
'It could happen to anyone.' Kostya brings out the contrast between 'with' and 'whom' in a few short words.
Ну, опоздал, ну, я больше не буду.
'Okay, I was late, I will not do it again.' Nastya brings out the contrast between 'come on' and 'was late' in a few short words. Max answers right away.
Не очень.
'Not really.' The meaning hinges on 'not' working together with 'very' in spoken Russian.
Я хотел еще вчера вам об этом сообщить.
'I wanted to tell you about it yesterday.' The '-l' ending on the verb meaning 'wanted' places the action in the masculine past tense.
Но мы ж трубку не брали.
'But you were not picking up the phone.' Spoken Russian keeps this brisk, leaning on 'but' and finishing on 'took'. Max answers right away.
Елена Павловна!
'Elena Pavlovna!' In Russian, the idea of 'Elena' flows naturally into 'Pavlovna' without extra filler words.
Макс, кто разбил бутылку?
'Max, who broke the bottle?' Kostya raises the pitch on 'bottle' to turn the phrase into a direct spoken question.
В смысле?
'What do you mean?' Nastya raises the pitch on 'sense' to turn the phrase into a direct spoken question. Max answers right away.
Кристина ее разбила и сказала, что тебя уволит.
'Kristina broke it and said she is going to fire you.' Max anchors the line on 'Kristina', while 'will fire' completes the thought.
Если я с ней не пересплю.
'Unless I sleep with her.' Kostya brings out the contrast between 'if' and 'I' in a few short words.
С кем с Настей?
'Sleep with who, Nastya?' Notice how Russian expresses 'with' and 'Nastya' with crisp inflection rather than helper words. Max answers right away.
С Кристиной?
'With Kristina?' In Russian, the idea of 'with' flows naturally into 'Kris' without extra filler words. Alright, let's listen to all those lines again from the top.
